transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-01 16:00 UTC — 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen, Devon Patel (Redwood); Liam O'Connor, Priya Singh, Carlos Rivera (Spectral Payments)
Links shared: Optimize deck https://redwood.example.com/decks/optimize-batching.pdf ; cost model sheet https://redwood.example.com/sheets/cost-model-spectral (note: placeholder)

[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45-50 minutes today. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood team, and with me is Devon, our solutions engineer. We're going to run through batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations and then show the cost model that maps to Spectral's traffic.

[00:28] Liam: yeah thanks, excited. quick context — we ingest payment authorization messages, typical prompts ~220 tokens on average but some multi-turn flows push 1.5k tokens. latency SLO is 200ms p50; p95 can be up to 1s but we'd prefer lower.

[01:05] Devon: cool, that's helpful. one of the first tradeoffs is batching for throughput vs single-request latency. Redwood Optimize suggests continuous micro-batching which can hit per-token cost reductions while staying within latency SLOs. we'll show numbers.

[02:12] Priya: quick question — we run in GCP and are doing customer-sensitive stuff, so VPC+KMS is a must. we asked on the form about private deployments — where does caching live in a private deployment?

[02:40] Devon: good Q. in Private (VPC) deployments, the KV cache and prefix cache components are colocated with the inference nodes; keys are stored in memory with optional encrypted persistence to the host, and KMS integrates for any at-rest keys. for hosted, we offer multi-tenant caches with RBAC and audit logs. there can be subtle differences in cold-start behavior.

[03:30] Carlos: and how do you handle cache invalidation — if our embeddings change or user prompt formats evolve, will the prefix cache become stale?

[03:52] Devon: yep, prefix cache is best for stable prefixes — think system prompts, common boilerplate. keys are versioned per model revision and you can set TTLs or explicit invalidation hooks. many customers run short TTLs for user-specific data and longer TTLs for app-level prefixes.

[04:30] Maya: i'll flag that in the cost model sheet too — TTLs affect effective hit rate and therefore unit cost.

[05:00] Liam: can you show the numbers? like if we have 60% cache hit rate and batch size average of 4, what does that do to cost & latency?

[05:22] Devon: sure. so baseline — hosted API on xg-2 model (example) at 1.0 token cost unit. with batching of 4, effective per-token GPU time drops roughly 18-22% because of amortized kernel overheads. with a 60% KV hit rate, you only pay for 40% of tokens hitting the model, so combined you can see 40-50% unit cost reduction versus naive single-request no-cache.

[06:45] Devon: caveat — batching increases tail latency if you wait to fill a batch. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching with latency budgets per route so you can cap the wait time (e.g., 20ms) to keep p95 low.

[07:20] Priya: that latency budget — is that per-tenant configurable? can we set stricter budgets for high-priority routes?

[07:34] Devon: yes, per-route policies are supported; you can set a strict latency SLO which will force smaller batch windows or route to a lower-cost but faster variant.

[08:05] Carlos: how about cold-starts? we have bursty traffic mornings and nights. will caching warm things up automatically?

[08:24] Devon: the prefix cache helps with warm starts for repeated prompts; for KV cache, warmup depends on your access patterns. Redwood also supports proactive cache prefill as part of Dedicated on-boarding — we can pre-populate hot keys based on your trace.

[09:12] Liam: you mentioned model variants and fallbacks — if dedicated capacity is exhausted, can we fallback to hosted with degraded QoS?

[09:25] Maya: yes, routing policies support tiered fallbacks — you can prefer Dedicated, then Hosted Reserved, then Shared. we also do automatic model-variant fallback (quantized variant) if exact variant not available.

[10:05] Devon: back to numbers — i'll walk through a simple cost model. assume 10M monthly tokens, average prompt length 220 tokens, 30% of requests benefit from prefix cache, and KV hit rate 60% for the cached portion. that yields an effective model token count of ~4.2M tokens and network/overhead tokens are separate. factor in batching (avg size 3.8) and you get roughly 42% cost savings.

[11:00] Priya: these assumptions are sensitive — we have some flows with 1500 token contexts; how does that change throughput?

[11:20] Devon: for long contexts, KV cache still helps if the large part is repeated; batching efficiency sometimes drops because long requests occupy GPU longer, but we can use seq-length-aware kernel selection and route long requests to dedicated pools optimized for large seqs.

[12:05] Liam: security: SOC2? full audit logs? SSO integration?

[12:15] Maya: yes SOC2 Type II, ISO27001 package available; we provide audit logs per request, SAML SSO, RBAC in Console; for Private you can integrate KMS/HSM. i'll share the security pack after the call.

[12:40] Carlos: any customers in fintech with similar profiles?

[12:50] Maya: we have several payment and banking customers; i'll include anonymized case notes and a customer reference list in the follow-up.

[13:10] Devon: quick demo — i'm sharing my screen, the Optimize console. here you can see per-route latency budgets, batching window sliders, cache hit rate metrics, and the cost breakdown by tokens + infra.

[13:40] Devon: see this trace — the cost model tab links your token distribution to per-hour compute costs; if you bump TTL to 6 hours from 30 minutes you'll see the hit rate rise but also potential stale-data risk.

[15:00] Priya: what's the recommended TTL for auth-like prompts? short-lived tokens are sensitive.

[15:12] Devon: for auth prompts we recommend short TTLs (minutes) or no KV caching for user-specific sensitive tokens; prefix cache is safe for static system prompts. also you can encrypt cache at rest and limit which services can read the cache.

[16:05] Liam: can we see an end-to-end benchmark? like run our sample traffic against Redwood Dedicated with these caching configs?

[16:20] Maya: yes — action item: we'll run a 24h benchmark using your sample traces. Devon will own the run, and Maya will share the reserved capacity pricing and the cost model spreadsheet filtered to your traffic.

[16:45] Devon: one more thing on cost modeling: include network egress and request routing costs in your internal TCO. sometimes teams discount those and then are surprised.

[17:10] Priya: do you support custom quantized model variants for very high throughput?

[17:20] Devon: yes, Dedicated supports custom quantization profiles; we also recommend model distillation or smaller decoder variants for high-RPS paths. Redwood Optimize will recommend candidate quantization and show expected quality delta — we can do A/B evals as part of the pilot.

[18:05] Carlos: latency vs cost tradeoffs — is there a simple chart we can include in an internal doc?

[18:14] Maya: i'll export the chart from the cost model and send it; we'll include p50/p95 impact at different batching windows and hit rates.

[19:00] Liam: timelines — if the benchmark looks good, what does a pilot look like?

[19:12] Maya: pilot typically 4-8 weeks: setup dedicated pool, migrate a single route, run parallel traffic, check metrics and cost, then expand. if you want reserved capacity commit we'll price accordingly.

[20:05] Priya: legal/procurement questions — we have a standard fintech DPA and need data residency controls.

[20:20] Maya: legal will loop in our contracts team; we support region pinning for data residency and can add provisions in the DPA. i'll cc contracts on the security pack email.

[21:10] Devon: quick note on observability: Console exposes token-level cost, trace-level latency, and a prompt-regression alerting hook. that helps detect if a cache change caused quality regressions.

[22:00] Liam: what about model-versioning risk — if you rollout a new model that changes outputs, can Optimize run evals automatically?

[22:15] Devon: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic evals using your labeled prompt set. we can do differential comparisons and rollback on regressions.

[23:05] Priya: ok this is helpful. couple of nitty gritty Qs: do you have a prefill API for KV? and is the cache size configurable per route?

[23:20] Devon: yes and yes. prefill API accepts key/value pairs and we allow per-route cache sizing and eviction policies.

[24:05] Carlos: what about monitoring — will we get alerting for cache hit rate drops?

[24:18] Devon: yep, Console has alerts for hit-rate, latency regressions, and cost spikes. alerts can integrate with pagerduty or slack.

[25:00] Maya: recap and next steps — we'll: 1) run 24h benchmark (Devon), 2) send pricing/reserved capacity options + cost model (Maya), 3) Spectral to share traffic traces and SLOs (Priya). propose follow-up 2027-11-12 to walk results.

[26:15] Liam: sounds good. quick FYI — we also evaluate Anthropic for safety reasons, but cost is a big factor so this is helpful.

[26:40] Maya: noted — we'll include competitor positioning in the follow-up.

[27:00] Priya: last Q — down the road we may want on-prem for compliance. do you support air-gapped installs?

[27:10] Maya: yes, Private supports on-prem with an offline installer and local control plane. that's a different commercial motion but doable.

[27:45] Devon: i'll drop a short runbook describing the benchmark steps and the credential exchange.

[28:10] Carlos: thanks all, that covers our main concerns. we'll aim to get the traces to Priya and she'll upload to the secure bucket you provide.

[28:30] Maya: great, i'll follow up with security docs and the pricing sheet. thanks for your time.

[28:45] Liam: thanks, appreciate it.

-- End of recording (note: transcription imperfect; some proper nouns may be mis-transcribed)
